explanation:
[EFFECT] The day of the week has a non-monotonic, categorical effect on predicted bike demand — it does not rise or fall steadily from Sunday to Saturday. Instead, the two weekend days (Sunday = 0 and Saturday = 6) produce the widest swings: at certain hours they push predicted demand significantly higher (SHAP contributions up to about +0.6), while at other hours they pull it sharply lower (down to roughly −0.9 on Sundays). Midweek days (Monday through Thursday) show a more moderate and narrower spread of contributions, with positive peaks around +0.25 to +0.45. Friday and Saturday tend to show slightly higher positive contributions than the core working days, while Sunday carries the most negative tail of any day.

[IMPORTANCE] Weekday is the **4th most important** feature out of all 9, with an importance score of 0.173. It is meaningfully influential, though it sits well below the hour of the day (0.833) and is roughly on par with temperature (0.197) and year (0.200) — so it explains a solid share of demand variation but is not the dominant driver.

[RECOMMENDATION] Because weekend and weekday demand patterns differ substantially — with weekends showing stronger leisure-driven hourly swings rather than clear commuter peaks — the company should consider maintaining different bike distribution and staffing schedules for weekdays versus weekends, rather than applying a one-size-fits-all plan across the whole week.
